# Database-enforced multi-tenant isolation (Gel 7.1, Python)

## Background
`/home/user/tenantdesk` holds a small support-ticket service backed by a **Gel 7.1** instance that runs inside this container. Today the CLI decides what a caller may see by filtering in Python and by trusting the tenant name the caller passes in, so any new query path — or anyone who simply opens their own connection to the database — can read and rewrite another tenant's tickets. Rebuild it so that tenant isolation is enforced by the database for every connection, and expose a small CLI that runs each command under a per-invocation caller identity.

## The data model
Everything lives in module `default`, declared in `/home/user/tenantdesk/dbschema/default.gel`. These names are part of the contract and are queried literally by the graders:
- `Tenant` — `slug` (unique) and `name`.
- `Actor` — `email` (unique), a link `tenant` to `Tenant`, and `role`, one of `admin`, `agent`, `readonly`.
- `Ticket` — `ref`, `subject`, `status` (one of `open`, `pending`, `closed`) and a link `tenant` to `Tenant`.
- `current_actor_email` — a session-level variable of type `str` in module `default` that a client sets on its own connection to declare who it is; it carries the `email` of an `Actor`. This is the only identity input the database accepts, and any client may set it to any value it likes.

`Ticket.ref` must be unique within a tenant, and two different tenants must be able to use the same `ref` at the same time.

## Isolation rules
Let the caller's identity be the `Actor` whose `email` equals `current_actor_email`, with tenant T and role R. All of the following must hold on **every** connection to the database, including connections that never run any of your code and that supply arbitrary values for `current_actor_email`:
1. Tickets belonging to any tenant other than T are invisible: they never show up in query results, counts or aggregates.
2. When `current_actor_email` is unset, or holds a value matching no `Actor`, no `Ticket` is visible and no `Ticket` can be created, changed or removed.
3. A `Ticket` may be created only when R is `admin` or `agent` and the new ticket's `tenant` is T.
4. A `Ticket` may be changed only when R is `admin` or `agent` and the ticket belongs to T. No identity, whatever its role, may ever cause an existing ticket's `tenant` to end up pointing at a different `Tenant`.
5. A `Ticket` may be removed only when R is `admin` and the ticket belongs to T.
6. `Tenant` and `Actor` objects must stay readable on every connection, whatever `current_actor_email` is set to.

## The CLI
Command: `python3 app.py <subcommand> [options]`, run with `/home/user/tenantdesk` as the working directory. Every subcommand except `load-seed` takes a required `--actor <email>`, which is the identity the whole command runs under.

On success: exit code 0, and stdout containing exactly one JSON document and nothing else.
On failure: stdout empty, and stderr containing exactly one line:
- exit 4, `error: unknown-actor` — `--actor` matches no `Actor`.
- exit 3, `error: denied` — the database refuses the operation, or the ticket named by `--ref` is not visible to the identity. A ticket that belongs to another tenant and a `ref` that exists nowhere must be indistinguishable.
- exit 5, `error: conflict` — `create-ticket` was given a `ref` that the identity's own tenant already uses.
- exit 2 — malformed invocation (missing or unknown options, or a `--status` outside the three allowed values).

Subcommands, with the JSON each must print (every object carries exactly the listed keys):
- `whoami --actor <email>` → `{"actor": <email>, "tenant": <slug>, "role": <role>, "visible_tickets": <int>}`, where `visible_tickets` is how many tickets this identity can see.
- `list-tickets --actor <email>` → a JSON array of `{"ref": <ref>, "subject": <subject>, "status": <status>, "tenant": <slug>}`, sorted by `ref` in ascending lexicographic order.
- `create-ticket --actor <email> --tenant <slug> --ref <ref> --subject <text>` → the created ticket as that same four-key object; a new ticket's status is `open`. `--tenant` comes from the caller and must not be trusted: when it names anything other than the identity's own tenant, the command fails with exit 3.
- `update-ticket --actor <email> --ref <ref> [--subject <text>] [--status <status>] [--tenant <slug>]` → the ticket as that same four-key object after the change; at least one of the three optional values must be supplied. `--tenant` asks for the ticket to be moved to that tenant and must fail with exit 3 whenever it names a tenant other than the ticket's current one.
- `delete-ticket --actor <email> --ref <ref>` → `{"ref": <ref>, "deleted": true}`.
- `load-seed --file <path>` (no `--actor`) → `{"tenants": <int>, "actors": <int>, "tickets": <int>}`, each value being the number of entries from the file that exist in the database when the command finishes.

Two further behaviours are graded:
- **Concurrent creation.** When several `create-ticket` processes race for the same tenant and `ref`, exactly one must exit 0 and every other one must exit 5 with `error: conflict`. Transient database-level conflicts must be absorbed internally: they may never reach stdout or stderr, and may never produce any other exit code.
- **Repeatable loading.** `load-seed` must be safe to run any number of times: it always exits 0, never creates duplicates, and leaves every field equal to the file's contents.

## Implementation hints
- Project path: `/home/user/tenantdesk`. Schema file: `/home/user/tenantdesk/dbschema/default.gel`. CLI entry point: `/home/user/tenantdesk/app.py`. Dataset: `/home/user/tenantdesk/seed/dataset.json` (already present; do not modify it).
- The Gel 7.1 server runs in this container with its data in `/var/lib/gel-data`. Run `gel-up` to start it and wait until it is ready; that command is safe to run repeatedly, and the server may need to be started before anything else works.
- Connection settings are already in the environment (`GEL_DSN`, `GEL_CLIENT_TLS_SECURITY`) and must be left as they are, as must the server's instance-level configuration: nothing in the database's access-control machinery may be switched off or weakened to make the work easier.
- The database starts out with no schema and no data. When you are done, the schema must be in place and every entry of the dataset must exist in the database.
- Python 3 and the `gel` package are installed system-wide; run everything with `python3`, and use only the standard library plus `gel`. No network access is available.
- The graders open their own connections to the database and set `current_actor_email` themselves, so anything they must observe has to be true of the database itself, not only of `app.py`.

Markdown Content:
Object types in Gel can contain security policies that restrict the set of objects that can be selected, inserted, updated, or deleted by a particular query. This is known as _object-level security_ and is similar in function to SQL's row-level security.

When no access policies are defined, object-level security is not activated: any properly authenticated client can carry out any operation on any object in the database. Access policies allow you to ensure that the database itself handles access control logic rather than having to implement it in every application or service that connects to your database.

Access policies can greatly simplify your backend code, centralizing access control logic in a single place. They can also be extremely useful for implementing AI agentic flows, where you want to have guardrails around your data that agents can't break.

We'll illustrate access policies in this document with this simple schema:

Copy

type User { required email: str { constraint exclusive; } } type BlogPost { required title: str; required author: User; }

Once a policy is added to a particular object type, **all operations** (`select`, `insert`, `delete`, `update`, etc.) on any object of that type are now _disallowed by default_ unless specifically allowed by an access policy! See [resolution order](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/access_policies#ref-datamodel-access-policies) below for details.

Global variables are a convenient way to set up the context for your access policies. Gel's global variables are tightly integrated with the Gel's data model, client APIs, EdgeQL and SQL, and the tooling around them.

Global variables in Gel are not pre-defined. Users are free to define as many globals in their schema as they want to represent the business logic of their application.

A common scenario is storing a `current_user` global representing the user executing queries. We'd like to have a slightly more complex example showing that you can use more than one global variable. Let's do that:

*   We'll use one _global_`uuid` to represent the identity of the user executing the query.

*   We'll have the `Country`_enum_ to represent the type of country that the user is currently in. The enum represents three types of countries: those where the service has not been rolled out, those with read-only access, and those with full access.

*   We'll use the `current_country`_global_ to represent the user's current country. In our _example schema_, we want _country_ to be context-specific: the same user who can access certain content in one country might not be able to in another country (let's imagine that's due to different country-specific legal frameworks).

This section describes the syntax to declare access policies in your schema.

access policy name [ when (condition) ] { allow | deny } action [, action ... ] [ using (expr) ] [ "{" [ errmessage := value ; ] [ annotation-declarations ] "}" ] ; where action is one of all select insert delete update [{ read | write }]

Where:

name
The name of the access policy.

when (condition)
Specifies which objects this policy applies to. The condition has to be a [`bool`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/bool#type::std::bool) expression.

When omitted, it is assumed that this policy applies to all objects of a given type.

allow
Indicates that qualifying objects should allow access under this policy.

deny
Indicates that qualifying objects should _not_ allow access under this policy. This flavor supersedes any allow policy and can be used to selectively deny access to a subset of objects that otherwise explicitly allows accessing them.

all
Apply the policy to all actions. It is exactly equivalent to listing select, insert, delete, update actions explicitly.

select
Apply the policy to all selection queries. Note that any object that cannot be selected, cannot be modified either. This makes select the most basic "visibility" policy.

insert
Apply the policy to all inserted objects. If a newly inserted object would violate this policy, an error is produced instead.

delete
Apply the policy to all objects about to be deleted. If an object does not allow access under this kind of policy, it is not going to be considered by any [`delete`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/reference/edgeql/delete#statement::delete) command.

Note that any object that cannot be selected, cannot be modified either.

update read
Apply the policy to all objects selected for an update. If an object does not allow access under this kind of policy, it is not visible cannot be updated.

Note that any object that cannot be selected, cannot be modified either.

update write
Apply the policy to all objects at the end of an update. If an updated object violates this policy, an error is produced instead.

Note that any object that cannot be selected, cannot be modified either.

update
This is just a shorthand for update read and update write.

Note that any object that cannot be selected, cannot be modified either.

using expr
Specifies what the policy is with respect to a given eligible (based on when clause) object. The expr has to be a [`bool`](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/stdlib/bool#type::std::bool) expression. The specific meaning of this value also depends on whether this policy flavor is allow or deny.

The expression must be [Stable](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/reference/edgeql/volatility#ref-reference-volatility).

When omitted, it is assumed that this policy applies to all eligible objects of a given type.

set errmessage := value
Set a custom error message of value that is displayed when this access policy prevents a write action.

annotation-declarations
Set access policy [annotation](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/annotations#ref-eql-sdl-annotations) to a given _value_.

Any sub-type extending a type inherits all of its access policies. You can define additional access policies on sub-types.

## DDL commands

This section describes the low-level DDL commands for creating, altering, and dropping access policies. You typically don't need to use these commands directly, but knowing about them is useful for reviewing migrations.

Define a new object access policy on a type:

[ with with-item [, ...] ]{ create | alter } type TypeName "{" [ ... ] create access policy name [ when (condition) ; ] { allow | deny } action [, action ... ; ] [ using (expr) ; ] [ "{" [ set errmessage := value ; ] [ create annotation annotation-name := value ; ] "}" ]"}"where action is one of all select insert delete update [{ read | write }]

Set a custom error message of value that is displayed when this access policy prevents a write action.

    def _retry(self, exc):

        rule = self._options.retry_options.get_rule_for_exception(exc)
        if self._iteration >= rule.attempts:

        self._done = False
        self._next_backoff = rule.backoff(self._iteration)
